section.title: The Olivet Discourse
section.sectionRationale: Jesus' longest discourse in Mark answers the disciples' question about the coming destruction of the temple and the end of the age. He warns of deception, wars, persecution, and a great tribulation centred on Jerusalem, points to the coming of the Son of Man in glory to gather His elect, and drives home one refrain: no one knows the day, so stay awake. It prepares the disciples, and the church, for the long, hard interval before the end.
section.thesis: Between His first coming and His return, history will be marked by upheaval, deception, and persecution, yet the gospel must reach all nations and the Son of Man will come in glory to gather His own; therefore the abiding command is not to calculate the date but to be watchful, faithful, and unafraid.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the temple's fall foretold; the beginning of birth pains and the call to witness; the tribulation and the abomination of desolation; the coming of the Son of Man; and the lesson of the fig tree with the call to keep watch.

units.label: The temple's fall foretold
units.note: not one stone left on another

verses.text: As Jesus was leaving the temple, one of His disciples said to Him, “Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!”
“Do you see all these great buildings?” Jesus replied. “Not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.”
While Jesus was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked Him privately,
“Tell us, when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to be fulfilled?”

units.label: The beginning of birth pains
units.note: the gospel must be proclaimed to all nations

verses.text: Jesus began by telling them, “See to it that no one deceives you.
Many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am He,’ and will deceive many.
When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the {{telos|end}} is still to come.
Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places, as well as famines. These are the beginning of birth pains.
So be on your guard. You will be delivered over to the councils and beaten in the synagogues. On My account you will stand before governors and kings as witnesses to them.
And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations.
But when they arrest you and hand you over, do not worry beforehand what to say. Instead, speak whatever you are given at that time, for it will not be you speaking, but the Holy Spirit.
Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child. Children will rise against their parents and have them put to death.
You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.

units.label: The tribulation and the abomination
units.note: let those in Judea flee to the mountains

verses.text: So when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.
Let no one on the housetop go back inside to retrieve anything from his house.
And let no one in the field return for his cloak.
How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers!
Pray that this will not occur in the winter.
For those will be days of {{thlipsis|tribulation}} unseen from the beginning of God’s creation until now, and never to be seen again.
If the Lord had not cut short those days, nobody would be saved. But for the sake of the {{eklektos|elect}}, whom He has chosen, He has cut them short.
At that time if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘There He is!’ do not believe it.
For false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform signs and wonders to deceive even the elect, if that were possible.
So be on your guard; I have told you everything in advance.

units.label: The coming of the Son of Man
units.note: coming in the clouds with great power and glory

verses.text: But in those days, after that tribulation: ‘The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light;
the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.’
At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory.
And He will send out the angels to gather His elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.

units.label: The fig tree and the call to watch
units.note: keep watch, for you do not know the hour

verses.text: Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near.
So also, when you see these things happening, know that He is near, right at the door.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.
No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
Be on your guard and stay alert! For you do not know when the appointed time will come.
It is like a man going on a journey who left his house, put each servant in charge of his own task, and instructed the doorkeeper to keep watch.
Therefore keep {{gregoreo|watch}}, because you do not know when the master of the house will return, whether in the evening, at midnight, when the rooster crows, or in the morning.
Otherwise, he may arrive without notice and find you sleeping.
And what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!”

telos.gloss: The end, the goal or consummation. Jesus warns that wars and disasters are not yet the end but the beginning of birth pains; the end is the appointed climax of history when the Son of Man comes. Perseverance to the end, the same word, is the mark of the saved.

thlipsis.gloss: Tribulation, pressure, affliction. Jesus foretells a time of unequaled distress centred on Jerusalem, and more broadly the pressures the church endures until the end. God limits the days for the sake of His chosen ones, so that tribulation, though severe, is bounded by His mercy.

eklektos.gloss: The elect, the chosen. God's chosen people are the reason the days of tribulation are shortened and the ones the Son of Man gathers at His coming. Their election secures them through deception and distress; even the most cunning false prophets cannot finally lead them astray.

gregoreo.gloss: To stay awake, be watchful, be alert. The refrain of the discourse, keep watch, is not anxious date-setting but wakeful, faithful readiness, living each day as those who expect their Master and do not want to be found asleep when He returns.

basic.context: As they leave the temple, a disciple admires its massive stones, and Jesus stuns them: not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives, four disciples ask when this will happen and what the sign will be. Jesus answers with a sweeping discourse. First, do not be deceived by false messiahs, wars, and disasters; these are only the beginning of birth pains, and meanwhile the gospel must reach all nations through persecuted witnesses. He warns of a terrible tribulation and an abomination of desolation, urging flight from Judea. He points beyond it to the coming of the Son of Man in glory to gather His elect. Then, with the fig tree, He teaches that the signs mean He is near, that this generation will see these things, and that no one knows the day or hour, so the command is: keep watch.
basic.hermeneutics: The discourse weaves together the near future, the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, and the ultimate future, Christ's return, so that the destruction of the temple becomes a preview of the end. The disciples asked one question, but Jesus answers on two horizons. The dominant note is not a timetable but readiness: watch, endure, do not be deceived, keep witnessing. Care is needed to distinguish what was fulfilled in that generation from what awaits Christ's return.
basic.originalLanguages: Wars are not yet the telos, the end, but birth pains; the one who endures to the telos will be saved. Jesus foretells a thlipsis, tribulation, shortened for the sake of the eklektos, the elect. And the refrain is gregoreo, keep watch.
basic.typology: The abomination of desolation draws on Daniel's prophecy, and the darkened sun and falling stars use the prophets' imagery of God's judgment. The Son of Man coming in clouds fulfils Daniel 7, receiving the kingdom.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Son of Man of Daniel 7 who will come in glory to gather His people, the prophet whose words outlast heaven and earth, and the Master who will return to His watching servants.
basic.god: God is sovereign over history's upheavals and mercifully limits the days of distress for His elect's sake. The Father alone knows the day. God's word through His Son will never pass away.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 7, 9, and 12 supply the Son of Man and the abomination. Isaiah 13 and Joel 2 give the darkened heavens. 1 Thessalonians 5 echoes the call to be awake.
basic.oneStory: Between the cross and the consummation stretches an age of upheaval, mission, and suffering, all held in God's hands. The temple that pointed to God's presence will fall, but the Son of Man will come in glory to gather His people from the ends of the earth. Until then, the church lives awake, enduring and witnessing, sure that Christ's words will never fail and His return is certain.

context.literary:
Mark 13 is the only long block of teaching in Mark's Gospel, and it is placed at a hinge. It follows the temple scenes of chapters 11 and 12, which end with a poor widow giving all she has to a building about to fall, and it leads straight into the passion narrative of chapters 14 to 16. The discourse is framed by the temple at both ends: it begins with the prophecy that the stones will be thrown down, verse 2, and it is answered by the charge in Mark 14:58 that Jesus said He would destroy this temple, and by the tearing of the veil in Mark 15:38. The question, 'when will these things happen, and what will be the sign?' in verse 4 is therefore not a detour from the story but a signal of what is coming.

The discourse is shaped by one word that returns over and over: watch. The Greek verb blepo, 'see to it,' opens verses 5, 9, 23 and 33, and the commands to stay awake close it, verses 34 to 37. Between those alarms are three movements. Verses 5 to 13 describe what is not yet the end: deceivers, wars, quakes, persecution, and the gospel's spread. Verses 14 to 23 narrow to a single crisis, the abomination in Judea and a tribulation without precedent. Verses 24 to 27 lift the eyes beyond it to the Son of Man in the clouds. Verses 28 to 37 then turn from prediction to instruction through two parables, the fig tree and the doorkeeper.

The language shifts register as it goes. Verses 5 to 23 are largely warning in the second person, 'you will be delivered,' 'you will stand,' 'let those in Judea flee.' Verses 24 to 27 are in the third person and in the poetry of the prophets. The effect is that readers are pulled into the story's pressure and then lifted above it.
context.historical:
The temple the disciples admire was Herod's rebuilding, a vast complex of white stone, gold and colonnades that was still under construction in Jesus' day. To a Galilean pilgrim it looked as unmovable as the mountain it stood on. When Jesus says the stones will be thrown down, He speaks in the tone of Jeremiah, who warned that the house would become like Shiloh, Jeremiah 26:6, and Micah, who said Zion would be plowed like a field, Micah 3:12. Those prophets had also been accused of attacking the temple.

The place of the discourse matters. On the Mount of Olives the four disciples look across the valley at the temple, and the Mount of Olives is itself the place where Zechariah says the LORD will stand on the day He comes, Zechariah 14:4. Only Peter, James, John and Andrew are named as hearers, the first two pairs of brothers called at the lake in Mark 1:16-20, which gives the discourse a private, family flavour.

Within a generation of this scene Jewish revolt against Rome began and ended in the siege of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple in AD 70. The signs Jesus gives are not obscure to a first-century reader. False messiahs promised deliverance; the empire was convulsed by wars and civil strife; there were famines and earthquakes. Believers were handed over to local councils and synagogue courts, as Mark's own readers could testify, and they were hauled before governors and kings.

Luke's version of the warning reads 'when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies,' Luke 21:20, which shows how at least one early interpreter read the abomination of desolation in the light of the Roman siege. Flight to the mountains was the common instinct of villagers in Judea, and the instructions about the roof and the field are those of people who must flee with no time to pack.
context.canonical:
The discourse is thickly woven from the Old Testament. The abomination of desolation comes from Daniel, who uses it for the desecration of the temple in the days of the Greek tyrant, Daniel 11:31, and also for something still ahead, Daniel 9:27 and 12:11. Jesus tells the reader to understand, which sends us back to Daniel. The tribulation of verse 19 echoes Daniel 12:1, 'a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred,' and the eventual deliverance of Daniel's people. The darkened sun and moon and falling stars, verses 24 and 25, draw on the prophets' language of judgment on cities and nations, Isaiah 13:10, Isaiah 34:4 and Joel 2:10. The Son of Man coming with the clouds is Daniel 7:13-14, where He is given an everlasting dominion. The gathering of the elect from the four winds recalls Deuteronomy 30:4 and Zechariah 2:6.

The discourse is also echoed throughout the New Testament. Matthew 24 and Luke 21 retell it with their own emphases; Matthew adds more parables of watchfulness in chapter 25. Paul draws on its images when he writes that the day of the Lord comes like a thief and that people will be caught like a woman in labour, 1 Thessalonians 5:1-6; he also takes over the instruction to stay awake and sober. Paul's warning that the man of lawlessness will seat himself in the temple, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, and John's picture of the coming one seen by every eye, Revelation 1:7, belong to the same cluster. Peter, writing to those who wondered why the promised day was delayed, answers that the Lord is not slow but patient, 2 Peter 3:8-10, speaking to exactly the tension this discourse creates between 'near' and 'not yet.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark writes for people who have already begun to live this chapter. Many of his first readers were under pressure, and some had probably seen what the war with Rome did to Judea or heard of it. He wants them to hear that none of it catches Jesus off guard. The prophecy of the temple's fall was given beforehand, and so were the warnings of false teachers, betrayal inside families, and trials before governors. The knowledge that Jesus said it first turns terror into a kind of steadiness: 'I have told you everything in advance,' verse 23.

Mark does not want his readers to treat the chapter as a code for working out the date. The repeated refrain is not 'calculate' but 'watch,' and the last paragraph says plainly that nobody knows the day, not even the Son, verse 32. Mark's own care is shown in the little aside, 'let the reader understand,' verse 14, which tells the reader to look at Daniel with care and not to rush to a conclusion.

The chapter also frames the passion. The disciples are told that they will be arrested, handed over, and hated for His name, and the same words, 'handed over,' are used of Jesus in the chapters that follow. Their suffering will follow His. Mark wants disciples to understand that a faithful life in the interval is a life of witness and endurance, and that the Son of Man whom they will watch suffer is the same one they are told to expect in glory.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is prediction, which means it describes what will happen and does not command it. Wars, quakes and famines are not instructions; they are the setting of the age. The commands are fewer and clearer: do not be deceived, do not be alarmed, speak what you are given when arrested, flee when the abomination appears, do not believe those who say 'Here is the Christ,' keep watch. These are the part of the discourse meant to be followed in every generation.

The flight instructions of verses 14 to 18 belong to people in Judea in a particular crisis, and they are not a call to every believer to run to hills or to pray against winter. The principle that carries forward is that Jesus' people can be given a way out and that wisdom, not bravado, belongs to the faithful. The statement about speaking whatever is given, verse 11, is a promise to those on trial, not a licence to skip preparation when preaching or teaching.

Above all, readers should resist reading headlines as the 'beginning of birth pains.' Jesus says that wars and earthquakes 'must happen' but that the end is not yet, verse 7. The same verse that tells us not to be alarmed also tells us not to be calculating. A date-setting reading of this passage runs against verse 32.

debates.question: What is the abomination of desolation, and when does it happen?

views.label: Events of AD 66 to 70
views.case: Many interpreters, ancient and modern, read it as the Roman armies and the pollution of the temple in the Jewish war, with Luke 21:20 as the interpretive key. The instruction to flee to the mountains and the phrase 'those who are in Judea' fit a local crisis, and the verb 'standing where it should not be' suits a profaning presence in the temple.

views.label: A future Antichrist figure
views.case: Others stress that the Greek participle for 'standing' is masculine although the noun 'abomination' is neuter, which suggests a person, and they link the passage to the man of lawlessness who takes his seat in God's temple, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4. On this view Daniel's sacrilege under Antiochus was a preview, and the final form is still to come.

views.label: A pattern that recurs and finds a climax
views.case: A third view holds that Daniel's prophecy has several stages: the second-century desecration, the events of AD 70, and a last, worse form at the end. Jesus' deliberate vagueness, 'let the reader understand,' suits a pattern that can repeat.

debates.bearing: Mark leaves the identification open on purpose. All three views agree on what Jesus asks of His hearers: recognise the sign, do not stay, and trust Him in the crisis. Whichever reading is adopted, the discourse is not meant to feed speculation about particular people or dates.

debates.question: What does 'this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened' mean?

views.label: The generation then living
views.case: The natural sense of 'this generation' in the Gospels is Jesus' contemporaries, and 'these things' refers to the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem that the disciples asked about, verses 2 to 4. The prediction was fulfilled in AD 70. Mark 9:1 is read in the same way.

views.label: The people or race
views.case: Some take 'generation' as 'nation' or 'race,' meaning that the Jewish people will not cease before the end. This is possible in Greek but less common in the Gospels, where the word usually means those alive at the time.

views.label: The generation that sees the signs
views.case: Others hold that 'this generation' means whoever witnesses the signs described in verses 5 to 25, so the saying is a promise of how fast the end will unfold once it begins. Verse 29, 'when you see these things happening,' is cited for this.

debates.bearing: All three readings fit with verse 31 and verse 32: Jesus' words are sure, and the date is not for us. The saying should be read as an assurance that His word will be vindicated, never as a calendar.

study.originalLanguages:
Mark's most characteristic word in this chapter is blepo, 'see to it,' which opens verses 5, 9, 23 and 33 and is used in the sense of take care, beware. Its repetition shows that the chapter is built as a series of alarms, not as a chart. Alongside it stands the group of words for staying awake, and verse 33 adds agrypneo, 'stay alert,' a verb of deliberate wakefulness. The same four disciples will meet the command again in the garden, where Jesus finds them sleeping, Mark 14:37-38.

The 'birth pains' of verse 8 are odin, the labour pangs of a woman giving birth. In the prophets this image is used for the sudden anguish that precedes a new thing, Isaiah 26:17-18 and 66:7-9. The word is not a picture of despair but of pain with a purpose, and John 16:21 uses the same logic: the woman's anguish gives way to joy. Paul takes it up in Romans 8:22 when he describes creation groaning together. The word does not promise that the pains are brief; it says they are the beginning of something.

'You will be delivered over' in verses 9 and 11 and 12 is paradidomi, 'hand over.' Mark uses the same verb for what Judas does to Jesus, Mark 14:10, and for what happens to Jesus in the passion. The disciples' fate is deliberately matched to their Lord's. The Greek for 'the one who perseveres,' ho hypomeinas, is a participle of waiting under pressure and not merely lasting it out.

The abomination of desolation, bdelygma tes eremoseos, translates a Hebrew phrase in Daniel built on shiqqutz, a detestable thing, and a verb of making desolate. The oddity in Mark is grammatical: the participle 'standing,' hestekota, is masculine though bdelygma is neuter, a deliberate break in agreement that makes a reader pause. The marginal comment, 'let the reader understand,' ho anaginosko noeito, is addressed to the one who reads, which is why many take it as Mark's, not Jesus', aside.

In verse 30 the verb 'pass away' is parerchomai, which appears again in verse 31 in an emphatic double negative, ou me. 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.' The phrase is an emphatic denial, and it rests the whole discourse on the permanence of what Jesus says. The 'gathering' of verse 27 is episynago, to gather in, the same verb used of a hen gathering chicks in Luke 13:34. Verse 4 uses synteleo, 'be fulfilled,' a word of completion that signals the end of a process.

typology.type: The temple whose stones are thrown down, 1 Kings 8 and Jeremiah 7
typology.fulfillment: Solomon's temple was the place where God put His name, and Jeremiah warned that trusting in it as a charm would not save the city, Jeremiah 7:14. Jesus announces the same about Herod's temple. The fall of the first temple in 586 BC and the second in AD 70 are two blows of the same kind, and each shows that a building cannot hold God's presence in place of obedience. In Christ the correspondence deepens, because He speaks of Himself as the temple to be raised in three days, Mark 14:58, and John says He spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:21. The type falls short in that the earthly temple was always a shadow, so its fall is not a loss to the people of God but the shadow giving way to substance, Hebrews 8:13.

Under the Greek king Antiochus, an idolatrous altar was set up in the temple and the daily offerings stopped, which Daniel's visions describe in advance. Jesus uses the phrase as a pattern for a coming profanation of the temple, and the Roman armies' arrival in AD 70 fits it. The escalation in Christ is that the sacrilege is judged by the Son of Man Himself, who is the true meeting place of God and humanity. The type falls short of the end, since the same phrase is seen again by Paul in the figure who sets himself up as God, 2 Thessalonians 2:4, so the pattern may reach further.

typology.type: The Son of Man coming with the clouds, Daniel 7:13-14
typology.fulfillment: Daniel sees a figure like a son of man go to the Ancient of Days and receive a kingdom that all peoples serve. In Mark, Jesus applies the vision to Himself, first in this discourse, verse 26, and again before the high priest, Mark 14:62. The correspondence is the same figure, the same clouds, the same authority. The escalation is that the Son of Man comes not just to receive the kingdom but to gather His people from the four winds. The vision, the New Testament says, begins at the ascension, Acts 1:9-11, and finishes at His appearing, Revelation 1:7, so the type is fulfilled in stages, not all at once.

typology.type: The fig tree and the signs of the season, Mark 13:28
typology.fulfillment: The fig tree is an everyday parable: when the branches soften and leaves come, summer is close. Earlier Mark has Jesus cursing a barren fig tree as a picture of a fruitless temple, Mark 11:12-21, and Joel and Hosea use fig imagery of Israel. The fig tree here is not a code for the nation; it is an ordinary tree that teaches ordinary wisdom. Its lesson in Christ is that the signs of His nearness are as readable as seasons, and that He Himself is the one at the door. It falls short of any timetable, since it teaches nearness, not date.

typology.type: The master who leaves a household and returns, Mark 13:34-37
typology.fulfillment: The man who goes on a journey and leaves servants in charge is a figure from many of Jesus' parables and echoes the owner of the vineyard in Mark 12:1. The picture is of a master whose return is certain and whose servants will be judged on faithfulness. In Christ the master is Himself the Son, and the household is the church, entrusted with His work until He comes. The parable falls short of a literal timetable: the watchfulness is the point, not the hour.

study.christ:
The discourse points to Christ first as the prophet whose word outlasts the world. Verse 31 says that heaven and earth will pass away but His words will not. In the Old Testament only God's word is spoken of in such terms, Isaiah 40:8, and Jesus takes that quality for His own. The disciples admire a temple that seems permanent, and He tells them that nothing visible is permanent but what He says.

It points to Him as the Son of Man of Daniel 7. In verse 26 the figure Daniel saw before the Ancient of Days is named as Jesus Himself, and what Daniel saw as a throne scene becomes a coming. This is the same title Jesus uses when He tells the disciples the Son of Man must suffer, Mark 8:31, and He uses it here of the same person in glory. The discourse thus sits between the two halves of His career: the rejection that is about to happen in Mark 14 and the vindication that will follow. The Son of Man who will be 'betrayed into the hands of sinners,' Mark 14:41, is the Son of Man who will come in the clouds.

It points to Christ as the shepherd of His elect. The elect for whom the days are shortened and whom the angels gather are His, verse 27, and His word to them is as pastoral as it is prophetic: do not be alarmed, speak what you are given, the Spirit will speak in you. The same Jesus who will be silent before His accusers promises that His people, when arrested, will not be left without a word.

It points to Him as the master who returns. The man who leaves and gives each servant a task is Jesus Himself, who will go and be gone for a time and then come back. The tasks given are real tasks, which means His absence is not idleness. Revelation 22:12 echoes the promise: 'Behold, I am coming soon.'

There is a hard saying to address honestly. In verse 32 Jesus says that no one knows the day, 'not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.' This does not cancel His deity. It reflects the humility of the Son who took on our nature, Philippians 2:6-8, and who in His incarnate life lived by the Father's direction, John 5:19. The Son has come as a servant who takes the Father's timetable as His own.

A caution applies. The discourse is not a hidden map of the last days with Jesus as one entry. It points to Him by what He says of His own coming, by the words that the New Testament quotes, and by His promises to His people.
study.god:
The first thing the discourse shows about God is that history is not out of His hands. Wars, famines and earthquakes feel like chaos, but Jesus calls them things that 'must happen,' verse 7, and the language of 'must' in Mark signals a purpose behind events. The word is the same used of the Son of Man who must suffer, Mark 8:31. The upheavals of the age are held inside a plan.

God is merciful in judgment. In verse 20 Jesus says that if the Lord had not cut short those days, no one would be saved, and that He cut them short 'for the sake of the elect, whom He has chosen.' Even the worst tribulation has a boundary, and the boundary is drawn out of kindness. The God of Daniel 12:1, who delivers everyone whose name is written in the book, is the same God here. Judgment is real, as the fall of the temple shows, but it comes within a mercy that keeps a people safe.

God is the one who knows. Verse 32 says that the day and hour are known by the Father alone. This is not ignorance in God but reserve: the Father keeps the time in His own authority, as Jesus says again in Acts 1:7. The refusal to hand out dates is also a form of care, since a world that knew the hour would either despair or doze. Instead, believers are asked to live in a trust that does not need a timetable.

God is faithful to His word. Verse 31 stakes everything on the permanence of Jesus' words, and the whole Bible stakes everything on the same. The prophecies given in advance, of the temple, of the persecution, of the Son of Man, show a God who tells His people what is coming so they will not be undone by it, as Isaiah 46:10 says He declares the end from the beginning.

God is patient and also near. The discourse holds two truths that seem to pull apart: the Lord is at the door, verse 29, and the Lord may be a long time, verses 34 to 36. Peter's answer, that the Lord is patient and not wishing that anyone perish, 2 Peter 3:9, explains why the delay is not neglect.

God is Trinity at work in the discourse: the Father alone knows the hour, the Son will come in glory, and the Holy Spirit will speak through witnesses on trial, verse 11. For worship, this means that believers need not be anxious: the One who ordained the story also writes the final page, and He wants His people awake, not afraid, as Paul says in 1 Thessalonians 5:4-6.

crossReferences.note: The vision behind verse 26. One like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus claims the vision for Himself in this chapter and again before the council in Mark 14:62, so Daniel's throne room scene becomes the Gospel's promise of His coming.

One of the three Daniel texts behind the abomination of desolation. It speaks of an end to sacrifice and an abomination on the wing of the temple, until the decreed destruction falls. Jesus' 'let the reader understand' sends the reader back to read Daniel with care.

The time of distress 'the likes of which will not have occurred,' with deliverance for everyone whose name is in the book. It is the source of the tribulation of verse 19 and carries the same hope for the elect of verse 20: the trouble is real, and so is the rescue.

The sun darkened, the moon withholding its light, stars losing their shine: Isaiah's picture of the day of the LORD against Babylon. Jesus borrows the picture in verses 24 and 25, which shows that cosmic language in the prophets is often used for the fall of great powers and the arrival of God's judgment.

Luke's parallel adds details that help interpret the discourse: Jerusalem surrounded by armies, Judea fleeing to the hills, the city trodden down until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. It is the strongest New Testament evidence that part of the discourse is about the events of the Roman siege.

A prophet at the temple gate warns that the house will become like Shiloh. The prophecy nearly cost Jeremiah his life. Jesus' words about the temple belong in the same line of prophets who spoke against the false security of a building, and who were hated for it.

On the day of the LORD, His feet stand on the Mount of Olives. It is a striking detail that Jesus gives this discourse from the same mountain, facing the temple, as though the place itself carries the promise of the day He describes.

The risen Lord answers the question about when with the same turn as here: it is not for you to know times and seasons, but you will be My witnesses. The disciples' curiosity is redirected to mission, as in Mark 13:10 where the gospel must first reach all nations.
Matthew's version of the line about the gospel in all the world adds that 'then the end will come.' It underlines that the church's mission, not date-setting, is the thing Jesus ties to the end.

Paul tells the Thessalonians that the day comes like a thief and like labour pains, and that they are children of the day who must stay awake and sober. This is the clearest apostolic restatement of verses 33 to 37 and shows the church taking the call to watch as its standing order.

The man of lawlessness seats himself in God's temple and claims to be God. Many link him to the abomination of Mark 13:14, which is why the debate over the sign includes a future figure. Paul's opening warning, 'Let no one deceive you,' matches Mark 13:5.

Peter answers scoffers who ask where the promised coming has gone. The Lord is not slow, a day is as a thousand years, and He is patient so that people may repent. It gives the theological reason the interval between the temple's fall and His return is longer than the disciples might have expected.

John's opening vision joins Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10: He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him. It is the book of Revelation's version of Mark 13:26 and shows how the early church read the Son of Man promise.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a garden where heaven and earth were joined, and the temple was always meant to be a small copy of that garden, a place where God dwells with His people. When Jesus tells the disciples that the temple will fall, He is saying that the long arrangement of shadows is ending. The building that stood for Eden, with its curtain, its cherubim and its guarded way in, has served its purpose, and the real thing is arriving in a person.

The fall's effects are on display in this discourse: deceivers, betrayal inside families, wars between nations, famine, earthquakes, and persecution. They are the symptoms of a creation that groans, Romans 8:22. Jesus calls them birth pains, which means they are neither the end of the world nor merely random but the sign of a delivery under way.

The discourse sits in the middle of redemption. The cross is days away, and the church's task in the age that follows is witness, to all nations, in the Spirit's power. The promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, is being carried out as the gospel goes to every people, verse 10. The Son of Man of Daniel's vision, who receives the kingdom, will come to gather His people from the four winds, and so the scattering that began at Babel, Genesis 11:8, and continued in exile, Deuteronomy 30:4, is undone.

The ending is the new creation. Heaven and earth, as we know them, will pass away, verse 31, but not in the sense of annihilation; Paul describes a creation set free from its bondage, Romans 8:21, and John sees a new heaven and a new earth, Revelation 21:1. The temple that falls here is not replaced by a better building but by the presence itself: John sees no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The people who stayed awake in the long night, who testified under pressure, endured to the end and were gathered, will live in the place where there is no more mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4.

Until then the church lives between the two comings. It does not know the hour, but it knows the Master, and the Master has given each servant a task. The refrain that closes the chapter, 'Keep watch,' is not a call to fear but a call to faithful work in the light of a certain return.

quiz.q: What did Jesus foretell about the temple?

options.text: That not one stone would be left on another; it would be completely thrown down.
options.note: Mark 13:2; fulfilled when Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70.

options.text: That it would be cleansed and restored to its former glory.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus foretold its total destruction.

options.text: That it would face judgment and ruin.
options.note: True in substance, but Jesus specified that not one stone would be left on another.

options.text: That it would be rebuilt larger than before.
options.note: Jesus predicted its destruction, not a grander rebuilding.

quiz.q: How does Jesus tell the disciples to regard wars, disasters, and false messiahs?

options.text: As the beginning of birth pains, not yet the end; they should not be deceived or alarmed.
options.note: Mark 13:6-8; these are the start of birth pains, and the end is still to come.

options.text: As certain signs that the end has already arrived.
options.note: Jesus says these things must happen but the end is still to come; they are not the end itself.

options.text: As troubles that precede the end, calling for calm and watchfulness.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should name them specifically as the beginning of birth pains.

options.text: As proof that God has lost control of history.
options.note: Jesus presents these as things that must happen under God's sovereign plan, not a loss of control.

quiz.q: What must happen among the nations before the end, and what awaits Jesus' witnesses?

options.text: The gospel must be proclaimed to all nations, and His witnesses will face persecution but be helped by the Spirit.
options.note: Mark 13:9-11; worldwide gospel proclamation amid persecution, with the Spirit speaking through them.

options.text: The gospel must be preached to all nations before the end.
options.note: True, but it omits the persecution of the witnesses and the Spirit's help that Jesus stresses.

options.text: The nations will all convert peacefully before the end.
options.note: Jesus foretells hatred and persecution, not universal peaceful conversion, alongside the gospel's spread.

options.text: The disciples should withdraw from the world and wait quietly.
options.note: They are sent to witness before governors and kings, not to withdraw.

quiz.q: What will the coming of the Son of Man be like?

options.text: He will come in the clouds with great power and glory and gather His elect from the ends of the earth.
options.note: Mark 13:26-27 draws on Daniel 7 for the glorious coming and gathering.

options.text: He will come quietly and secretly, known only to a few.
options.note: His coming will be visible and glorious, seen by all, not secret.

options.text: He will return in glory to gather His people.
options.note: True, but it should include the vivid detail of coming in the clouds with power and glory.

options.text: He will appear as one of many rival messiahs.
options.note: Jesus warns against false christs; His own coming will be unmistakable and glorious.

quiz.q: What is the central command of the discourse regarding the timing of the end?

options.text: No one knows the day or hour, so keep watch and stay ready.
options.note: Mark 13:32-37; since the time is unknown, the repeated command is to keep watch.

options.text: Calculate the signs carefully to determine the date.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus says no one knows the day and warns against being caught unready, not to set dates.

options.text: Since the time is hidden, live in constant, faithful readiness.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should state plainly that no one knows the day or hour.

options.text: Wait passively until unmistakable proof appears.
options.note: Jesus calls for active watchfulness and faithfulness, not passive waiting.

questions: Jesus warned repeatedly against being deceived. What voices or ideas today tempt you to be led astray about who Jesus is and what He requires?
The gospel must be proclaimed to all nations, often through suffering. How does this shape the way you view the mission of the church and your part in it?
Jesus promised that the one who endures to the end will be saved. Where do you most need endurance in your faith right now?
The Son of Man will come in glory to gather His people. How does the certainty of Christ's return steady you amid the turmoil of the world?
Jesus' final word is, keep watch. What would it look like to live this week awake and ready, rather than spiritually asleep?

translationNotes.note: The abomination of desolation draws on Daniel 9:27, 11:31, and 12:11; the aside let the reader understand invites careful discernment, and the phrase standing where it should not be points to the profanation of the holy place.

This generation will not pass away until all these things have happened points primarily to the events surrounding the temple's fall in AD 70, while the coming of the Son of Man reaches to Christ's final return.
The four watches of the night, evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning, mark the Roman division of the night and stress that the Master may come at any time.
